q: Which situation suits a waterfall approach best?
options: A regulatory change with a fixed, well-understood specification
A new mobile app where user needs are unclear
An experimental product with frequent pivots
A team that wants feedback every two weeks
why: Waterfall works when requirements are stable and well understood.

q: What is the main weakness of waterfall?
options: Misunderstandings are found late, when they are expensive to fix
why: Users see working software only near the end, so problems surface late.

q: In waterfall, how are changes to signed-off requirements usually handled?
options: Through a formal change request process
They are added to the next daily stand-up
Changes are not allowed under any circumstances
why: Waterfall uses formal change control after requirements are baselined.

q: Which is one of the four Agile Manifesto values?
options: Responding to change over following a plan
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
why: Agile values responding to change over following a plan. The other options reverse the values.

q: Does Agile mean 'no documentation'?
options: No; it means just enough documentation at the right time
No; agile requires more documents than waterfall
why: The manifesto values working software more, but still sees value in documentation.

q: In what year was the Agile Manifesto written?
why: It was written in 2001 in Snowbird, Utah.

q: A bank writes an up-front business case and high-level requirements, then delivers in two-week sprints. This is…
why: Hybrid approaches combine predictive planning with agile delivery and are very common.

q: What is the maximum length of a Scrum sprint?
why: The Scrum Guide says sprints are one month or less.

q: Who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog?
why: The PO owns the Product Backlog. BAs often help refine it.

q: What is the Scrum Master's main role?
options: Help the team use Scrum effectively and remove impediments
why: The Scrum Master is a servant-leader who coaches and removes blockers, not a task manager.

q: How long is the Daily Scrum?
why: The Daily Scrum is timeboxed to 15 minutes.

q: Which event focuses on improving how the team works?
why: The Retrospective is about the team's process. The Review is about the product increment.

q: At which event is the increment shown to stakeholders for feedback?
why: The Sprint Review inspects the increment with stakeholders and adapts the backlog.

q: Where does a BA usually fit in Scrum?
options: As one of the Developers or a close partner to the Product Owner
As a fourth official Scrum role
As the Scrum Master by default
why: Scrum has no BA role. BAs usually sit within the Developers or support the PO.

q: What is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog?
why: Product Backlog → Product Goal; Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal; Increment → Definition of Done.

q: The Definition of Done applies to…
options: Every item that becomes part of the increment
why: The DoD is a shared quality standard for all work.

q: Which is true about the Definition of Ready?
options: It is widely used but not part of the official Scrum Guide
It is one of the three Scrum artifacts
It is written by the Scrum Master only
why: DoR is a common team practice for when a story can enter a sprint, but the Scrum Guide doesn't define it.

q: Which item would typically appear in a Definition of Ready?
why: DoR checks whether a story is clear enough to start; acceptance criteria are a key part.

q: What do story points measure?
why: Story points are relative sizes, not time.

q: Why does Planning Poker have everyone reveal estimates at the same time?
options: To avoid anchoring on the first person's number
why: Simultaneous reveal prevents people being influenced by others, and differences prompt useful discussion.

q: Velocity is best used to…
options: Forecast how much the team can complete in future sprints
Compare the performance of different teams
why: Velocity is team-specific, so comparing teams' velocity is misleading.

q: A short, timeboxed investigation to reduce uncertainty before estimating is called…
why: Spikes answer technical or business questions so a story can be estimated.

q: A chart showing remaining work trending toward zero by sprint end is a…
why: Burndown charts show remaining work over time.

q: Backlog refinement is…
options: An ongoing activity to clarify, split, estimate and order backlog items
One of the five official Scrum events
Done only once at project start
The same as the Sprint Review
why: Refinement is continuous and not a formal event, though teams often schedule a session.

q: What is the main purpose of WIP limits in Kanban?
options: To expose bottlenecks and keep work flowing
why: Limiting work in progress reveals where work piles up and improves flow.

q: Which statement about Kanban is true?
why: Kanban is flow-based; it has no sprints or prescribed roles.

q: The time from a customer's request to its delivery is called…
why: Lead time covers the customer's whole wait. Cycle time starts when work begins.

q: A production-support team receives a steady stream of unplanned issues. Which approach fits best?
why: Kanban handles continuous, unpredictable work well.

q: In SAFe, what is PI Planning?
options: A joint planning event for many teams at the start of a Program Increment
why: PI Planning aligns teams on the objectives for the next increment, usually 8–12 weeks.

q: What does the horizontal line on a user story map usually mark?
options: The MVP or first release slice
why: Story maps slice horizontally into releases, starting with the MVP.

q: Which is a typical BA responsibility in an agile team?
options: Keeping the top of the backlog 'ready' with clear stories and acceptance criteria
why: BAs help refine and clarify backlog items so the team can deliver.

q: How does the BA role differ between agile and waterfall?
options: Agile BAs write requirements just in time and collaborate continuously
Agile BAs do no analysis at all
why: The core skills are the same; the timing and collaboration style differ.
